name: Mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration
aliases: neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 4

clinicalPearls: Usually autosomal recessive (occasionally autosomal dominant) NBIA caused by C19orf12 variants, with onset ranging from childhood to early adulthood.
A distinctive mix of upper and lower motor neuron signs, spastic paraparesis combined with a motor axonal neuropathy and amyotrophy, can closely mimic a motor neuron disorder.
Optic atrophy with progressive visual loss is a hallmark and is a key feature separating MPAN from PKAN.
Prominent neuropsychiatric features (behavioural change, emotional lability, impulsive or obsessive behaviour, and later psychosis) accompany a progressive dementia.
Parkinsonism and dystonia, often oromandibular, develop as the disease advances.

MRI shows T2 hypointensity (iron) in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra; a T2-hyperintense streak of the medial medullary lamina between the internal and external pallidum is characteristic, and the eye-of-the-tiger sign is usually absent.
Neuropathology combines iron deposition with Lewy bodies, hyperphosphorylated tau and axonal spheroids, so MPAN is both a synucleinopathy and a tauopathy.
C19orf12 encodes a small mitochondrial membrane protein implicated in lipid and fatty-acid metabolism, placing MPAN mechanistically near the coenzyme A pathway of PKAN.
reference.pathophysiology: C19orf12 encodes a small, highly conserved mitochondrial membrane protein whose precise function remains incompletely defined but which is implicated in lipid and fatty-acid homeostasis and, indirectly, in coenzyme A-related metabolism, linking it mechanistically to the pathway disrupted in pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration. Loss of functional protein produces mitochondrial dysfunction and disturbed lipid handling, and is followed by progressive iron accumulation in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra together with widespread neurodegeneration. The neuropathology is notable for co-existing alpha-synuclein-positive Lewy bodies, hyperphosphorylated-tau inclusions and axonal spheroids, reflecting combined failure of protein aggregation clearance and axonal integrity. This broad pathology explains the clinical convergence of pyramidal, extrapyramidal, lower motor neuron, optic and neuropsychiatric features, and inheritance is predominantly autosomal recessive with rare dominant kindreds described.
additionalDifferentials: Other NBIA subtypes (PKAN, BPAN, PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration, FAHN)
Juvenile amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / motor neuron disease
Young-onset Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonian syndromes
Mitochondrial disease with optic atrophy (dominant optic atrophy spectrum)
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with iron-sensitive sequences (susceptibility-weighted/T2*) to demonstrate pallidal and nigral iron and the medial medullary lamina streak
C19orf12 testing, ideally within an NBIA gene panel
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to characterise the motor axonal neuropathy and denervation
Ophthalmological assessment with optical coherence tomography and visual evoked potentials for optic atrophy
Serum caeruloplasmin and copper studies to exclude Wilson disease
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness with bulbar or respiratory compromise
New psychosis or severe behavioural disturbance
Frequent falls and loss of ambulation from combined spasticity and neuropathy
reference.prognosis: MPAN is slowly progressive over one to several decades, leading to severe combined motor and cognitive disability and reduced life expectancy. Treatment is supportive only.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as hereditary spastic paraplegia or motor neuron disease because of the mixed pyramidal and neuropathic picture.
Expecting the eye-of-the-tiger sign, which is characteristic of PKAN rather than MPAN, and discounting the diagnosis when it is absent.
Overlooking optic atrophy, one of the most useful distinguishing clues.
Attributing the neuropsychiatric features to a primary psychiatric illness.
references: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) clinical references
management: No disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive and symptom-directed
Treat dystonia with anticholinergics, baclofen or botulinum toxin injections, with deep brain stimulation considered for refractory dystonia
Manage spasticity with antispasticity agents and physiotherapy, and address the motor axonal neuropathy, weakness and amyotrophy with rehabilitation, orthoses and mobility aids
Trial of levodopa for parkinsonian features, recognising that response is often limited
Psychiatric management of behavioural change, impulsivity and psychosis, with cognitive support for the progressive dementia
Low-vision support and ophthalmology follow-up for the progressive optic atrophy
Multidisciplinary neurology-led care with speech and language therapy, dietetics and palliative planning as disability advances
Autosomal recessive (occasionally dominant) genetic counselling and family testing for C19orf12 variants
